source_text: Plane monet Romanos omnibus potestatibus subjici, quia non sit potestas nisi a Deo, quia non sine caussa gladium gestet, et quia ministerium sit Dei; sed et ultrix, inquit, in iram ei qui malum fecerit. Nam et praemiserat: Principes enim non sunt timori bono operi, sed malo. Vis autem non timere potestatem? fac bonum, et laudem ab ea referes. Dei ergo ministra est tibi in bonum. Si vero malum facias, time. Ita, non in occasione frustrandi martyrii jubet te subjici potestatibus, sed in provocatione bene vivendi, etiam sub illarum respectu, quasi adjutricum justitiae, quasi ministrarum divini judicii, hic etiam de nocentibus praejudicantis. Dehinc et exequitur quomodo velit te subjici potestatibus, reddere jubens, cui tributum, tributum; cui vectigal, vectigal; id est quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari, et quae Dei, Deo; solius autem Dei homo. Condixerat scilicet Petrus, regem quidem honorandum; ut tamen tunc rex honoretur, cum suis rebus insistit, cum a divinis honoribus longe est; quia et pater et mater diligentur, cum Deo non comparabuntur. Caeterum, super Deum diligi nec animam licebit.
pass_a_gloss: It clearly warns the Romans to be subject to all powers, because there is no power except from God, because he does not bear the sword without cause, and because it is a ministry of God; but also an avenger, it says, in wrath to him who has done evil. For he had also sent ahead: For rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you want not to fear power? do good, and you will receive praise from it. Therefore, it is a minister of God to you for good. But if you do evil, fear. Thus, not on the occasion of frustrating martyrdom does it order you to be subject to powers, but in the provocation of living well, even under their regard, as if a helper of justice, as if a minister of divine judgment, here also prejudging concerning the harmful. Then also it follows how it wants you to be subject to powers, ordering to render, to whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax; that is, the things that are Caesar's, to Caesar, and the things that are God's, to God; but man is of God alone. Certainly, Peter had agreed, that the king is to be honored; yet the king is to be honored only when he persists in his own matters, when he is far from divine honors; because also father and mother are cared for, when they will not be compared to God. Moreover, to love more than God will not be allowed, nor the soul.

pass_b_english: The text issues a blunt warning to the Romans: submit to every authority, since no power exists except from God; the magistrate does not carry the sword for nothing, but serves as God's minister—and, the apostle adds, as an avenger who executes wrath on the evildoer. He had already laid the groundwork: 'For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad.' Do you want to have no fear of authority? Then do what is good, and you will win its approval. It is therefore God's minister for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid. So the command to submit is not meant to frustrate martyrdom; it is a provocation to live well, even under their gaze, as if they were allies of justice and ministers of divine judgment, here already passing sentence on the guilty. The apostle then spells out exactly how he wants you to submit: pay what you owe—tribute to whom tribute is due, tax to whom tax is due; in other words, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's, for a human being belongs to God alone (Romans 13:1-7). Peter agreed that the king deserves honor, but only so long as the king stays in his own lane and keeps his distance from divine honors; father and mother are to be cherished, provided they are not set on a par with God. Beyond that, no one—not even your own soul—may be loved more than God.

review.notes: Pass B fails on the translation of the final sentence. The Latin 'Caeterum, super Deum diligi nec animam licebit' is rendered in Pass A as 'Moreover, to love more than God will not be allowed, nor the soul' and in Pass B as 'Beyond that, no one—not even your own soul—may be loved more than God.' However, the Latin 'nec animam licebit' (nor will the soul be permitted/allowed) is a distinct clause. Pass B's interpretation 'no one—not even your own soul' introduces a semantic shift regarding the agency of 'licet' (it is permitted) and the subject 'anima'. More critically, Pass B fails the 'Completeness' and 'Agency' check regarding the phrase 'solius autem Dei homo' (but man is of God alone). Pass A translates this as 'but man is of God alone', whereas Pass B translates it as 'for a human being belongs to God alone', which is acceptable, but the subsequent handling of the Peter/King section contains a significant error in agency/meaning: 'cum suis rebus insistit' (when he persists in his own matters/affairs) is rendered in Pass B as 'so long as the king stays in his own lane', which is a colloquialism that obscures the specific Latin sense of 'insistens' in this context, though the primary failure is the final sentence's structural deviation from the Latin syntax.
reasons: Pass B's translation of 'nec animam licebit' as 'not even your own soul—may be loved' changes the grammatical structure of the Latin 'licet' (it is permitted) and the relationship between the two clauses compared to the source.
